summary:
Algeria is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is criminalised under the Penal Code of 1966 (Ordinance 66-156 of 8 June 1966). ILGA records the offence as covering both male/male and female/female relations, punishable by 2 months' to 2 years' imprisonment and fines of 500-2000 Algerian dinars. The US State Department's 2023 country report gives the same custodial range, 2 months' to 2 years' plus fines, for undefined "homosexual acts". The UK Home Office country-of-origin information report of 26 July 2026, covering developments since May 2025, confirms that the 1966 Penal Code remains the operative framework and that same-sex activity is prohibited as "acts of homosexuality" on the basis of a legal summary updated in June 2026.

Gender transition has no statutory route and is blocked in practice. Cairo 52 reports that Algeria has no legal framework for gender-affirming healthcare, that Penal Code articles 274 and 264 could be used against providers, and that the absence of any legal gender-recognition procedure means civil-status gender-marker changes are theoretically blocked. A fact-check published on 5 August 2024 rated as true the statement that Algeria prohibits medical and surgical gender-affirming care and prohibits being transgender.

Detention carries documented risk. The US State Department reports that prison authorities separate vulnerable persons but that LGBTQI+ detainees hold no specific legal protections, and that civil society describes discrimination against LGBTQI+ persons as compounded. The largest documented enforcement action in recent years followed a police raid on a private home in el-Kharoub, Constantine Province, on 24 July 2020, when 44 people were arrested, 9 women and 35 men, most of them university students, over an alleged gay wedding. On 3 September 2020 a court sentenced 2 of them to prison and 42 to suspended terms, treating party decorations and "gay appearance" as evidence.

NGOs document arrests within the LGBT+ community in Algeria with little published information on whether those arrested were transgender, so the trans-specific share of enforcement is not measurable from open sources.
tangentialFactors:
Attitudes measured in the surrounding society are restrictive. A BBC/Arab Barometer survey published on 23 June 2019, drawing on 25,000 respondents across 10 countries plus the Palestinian territories, found Algeria the exception where fewer than 50% of respondents accepted a woman as head of state; the same polling recorded "not religious" identification rising region-wide from 8% to 13% since 2013.

The 2024 fact-check rating on gender-affirming care was issued alongside the debunking of the false rumour that boxer Imane Khelif was transgender, a case in which Algerian public attention to transgender identity was mobilised around an unsubstantiated claim.

For visitors considering an asylum claim, the UK Home Office's current baseline is that refusals are rarely certifiable as clearly unfounded, so claims from Algeria are generally treated as capable of being serious rather than manifestly unfounded.
localsOnly:
Internal relocation is assessed by the UK Home Office as viable for gay men, while lesbians and trans women face societal difficulties even when moving within Algeria.

Providers of gender-affirming care operate without a legal framework and are exposed to Penal Code articles 274 and 264, which Cairo 52 describes as de facto criminalisation of that care.

With no legal gender-recognition procedure, Algerians cannot change the gender marker on civil-status documents, which affects identity papers, administrative dealings and any interaction where documents are checked.

Arrest data published by NGOs on the LGBT+ community does not identify which detainees were transgender, limiting the ability of residents to assess trans-specific exposure to policing.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether border or immigration screening checks gender markers against travel documents is not addressed in any source held for Algeria, so entry-stage outing risk is unresolved.

Neither hate-crime enhancement for offences targeting gender identity nor any specific protection for transgender detainees is sourced; the only detention-related finding is the general separation of vulnerable persons without LGBTQI+ specific legal protection.

The 500-2000 dinar fine band comes from ILGA's 2008 compilation. The 2026 UK Home Office report confirms the imprisonment range and the continuing force of the 1966 Penal Code but does not restate the fine amounts, so their current value is not independently confirmed here.

No source held documents partner or spousal recognition, marriage rules, or access to gender-related healthcare for visitors, and no source gives incident-level data on violence against transgender people in Algeria.
